L3.1.1.1Requisition raise and approve
19 tasks
  1. Draft the role
  2. Owner and raiser
  3. Three desks: HR reads the role, Procurement audits the suppliers, the lead signs the money
  4. Alongside at one rank, the lead after both
  5. Auto-clear inside policy, by name, with the reason
  6. Nobody signs their own
  7. Procurement names the suppliers; the release stays within them
  8. Published · Cancelled · Archived
  9. The chain read by desk, on the list, the row and the raise form
  10. Words change freely; money goes back through approval
  11. Words change on one that is out, and every supplier who received it is told
  12. The panel, and a discussion on the row
  13. FIXED 2026-09-22: the row said which desk a requisition waits on by reading approvals[0], which is the first row the database returned and was the waiting desk only by luck. It reads the desk that is actually outstanding now, names the other desk at that rank where two sign alongside, and says how many are left after this one — “Approved. Two more approvals to go.” A requisition waiting on a desk now also reaches that desk’s own queue; it was visible on the role and nowhere a person looks.
  14. FIXED 2026-09-22: a closed role could still be cancelled, from the row and through the door, which wrote a withdrawal reason onto a role that had already been settled. Both refuse it in a sentence now.
  15. FIXED 2026-09-22: a CLOSED requisition read “Draft” on the client’s requisitions list, in the tab for roles nobody has raised yet, because stageOf fell through to the draft branch for any status it did not name. It reads Archived with “closed without being filled” on the row — not a tab of its own, because “closed” and “cancelled” are one word to a reader and only one of them means somebody withdrew it. A role turned down at approval reads the same way and says so, since CHANGES_REQUESTED goes back to the manager to fix and a refusal is the end of that requisition. A status nobody has placed reads as finished rather than as never started: a stale role offered for editing invites work on something that is over, while a live one that looks settled is corrected by its own status the moment anybody opens it. And mayEdit is read off stageOf rather than off a second list of statuses — the two lists disagreeing is what produced the bug, and a CLOSED role was past changing and still being offered an edit. Patch from demand, applied and extended by regulatory in src/lib/requisition-stage.ts.
  16. FIXED 2026-09-22, DEMAND — /api/requirements loaded four fields and sent none of them. The route uses include, so approvalState, archivedAt, headcount and cancelReason were all on the row in memory and the response mapper dropped them, so nothing downstream of that list could tell a live role from one withdrawn last week — which is the waste the list exists to prevent. The mapping is one pure function now (src/app/api/requirements/visible.ts) rather than a gate written inline beside each field, because the inline form is why the next field added inherited nothing and the decision had to be made again from scratch, and was not. The visibility call, which is the real work: archivedAt, cancelReason and headcount go to everybody — whether a role is still live, and why it stopped, is the supplier’s own business, and headcount is what turns “archived” into “all three seats filled”. approvalState goes to the company that raised the role and is ‘’ for everybody else: which of a client’s desks has signed is the same class of fact as billMin and endClientCompany, both already gated the same way. An empty string is inert rather than merely absent — stageOf matches it against three named strings and falls past all three — so a supplier still reads OPEN, CANCELLED and ARCHIVED off the other two columns, and REJECTED, the one state that promotes a row to ARCHIVED, never reaches them. The argument for showing a supplier that approval is outstanding (it says do not submit yet) is answered without opening the chain: one derived boolean, paused, true only for a published role sent back for re-approval after a change to the money, which is the single state POST /api/submissions already refuses in that word. The list now says it before the afternoon’s work rather than after, carrying no desk and no name. Two bugs fell out on the way and are fixed with it: a role the client put away by hand while it was still OPEN read “Published” to every supplier, because archiving writes a date and deliberately never touches the status; and the same role went on offering Run matching and Distribute, both gated on that column. The words file was checked against stageOf and left alone, with the reasoning written into it: the client’s chip on the row is closedBecause — “closed without being filled” — so the two lists already agree on the row, and “Archived” is the name of a drawer. Renaming CLOSED to “Archived” on the supplier’s list would have put Filled and Archived side by side, two words at different levels, since a filled role is archived too.
  17. A role belongs to the company that is hiring — a client to itself, a seated office to the client that granted it, a prime or a bench vendor to its own firm. It used to resolve “the first client you place somebody at”, so an integrator’s own role was written onto its customer’s company with its approval chain and its cost center
  18. FIXED 2026-09-22: Requirement.status and Requirement.approvalState are strings with a documented value set rather than enums, so the comment beside each column is the only place the set is written down — and both were wrong. status did not name CANCELLED, which the cancel door has been writing; approvalState did not name CHANGES_REQUESTED, which lib/requisition-approval returns as nextState. Those are exactly the two values stageOf needs to tell a called-off role and one handed back from one nobody has raised, and it falls through to DRAFT for anything it does not name. Both comments now name the whole set, and the comment is read by a test against what the product actually writes rather than trusted: requirement-status-words walks every requirement.create/update in src, reads the nextState and nextStatus unions off the approval chain, and fails naming the file that writes a value the schema does not mention. DECIDED, ARCHITECT: they stay strings. An enum would not have caught either drift — both values were legal members somebody forgot to write down — and a @default on an enum is exactly as unable to say “nobody set this” as a @default on a string, which is an argument for nullability rather than for an enum. What it would buy is a migration against a paying client’s data, and another one each time this vocabulary moves, which it is still doing. Reasoning is beside the column in prisma/schema.prisma; revisit when the column stops moving.
  19. BUILT 2026-10-08, sign-up walk round three, demand’s part (8ea50d138): Needs attention offers a chip only where its page is on the reader’s own menu or something waits under it, and a one-person firm with an empty book is told to record the contract she has or wait to be put forward (decisions/chips); GET /api/timesheets, /api/program/budget and /api/program/org refuse a seat with no desk in a sentence naming no key and log each refused read, and a desk-less worker reads only their own weeks (program/no-desk)

L3.1.1.2Budget and rate band
8 tasks
  1. Check the cost object has money
  2. Set the band per invitation
  3. DEMAND DONE — the client’s own dashboard answers what two suppliers charge for one role: the lowest, the highest and the gap, at the rung the client pays, in minor units and one currency per role. lib/census-page’s rateSpread is imported rather than re-derived — rate variance in this product was by hiring manager and could not see that two firms are paid differently for one skill. A role one supplier fills is named in a sentence instead of shown as a gap of zero; a role priced in two currencies is never compared; a role a supplier never priced carries the caveat that the real gap can only be wider. A list and not a chart, and shown to the buying side only. src/app/api/program/route.ts, src/app/dashboard/program/page.tsx.
  4. A firm the client holds a contract with is on the supplier register whether or not an agreement is on file, and says “No agreement” in words with what to do about it — the dashboard named four firms where the register listed three, and the two now answer one question
  5. The headline counts everything the page shows needs somebody — the decisions waiting, a start paperwork will refuse, a supplier with people on site and no agreement on file — and names each in the sentence. It counted the approval queue alone until 2026-09-21, so a desk read “Nothing needs you today.” over a blocked start nine days out and a firm working with no paper between it and the client
  6. FIXED 2026-09-21: a first-run sentence is only printed where the list it sits under is actually empty. The Requirements panel lists every role open or drafted, whatever its age; the first-good number reads a thirty-day window with mirrors excluded — two populations on purpose — and its empty state said “No roles open yet. The number starts with the first one.” under two requirements, one of them published with two candidates on it. The cause underneath was a second company: the number read caller.company while the panel resolves the client, so a program office seated at a client was handed a number counted over its own requirements. It resolves the program the same way now. The route also counts what the list counts and passes it in, so an empty number says which silence it is: never opened anything, open but not yet inside the window, or open and nothing good has landed. Each sentence quotes its own scope rather than a count the list beside it disagrees with, and the page prints it only where the two agree there are roles at all.
  7. FIXED 2026-09-22: a program office seated at a client read the approval queue on the client’s page with no clause saying whose it was, so its own firm’s requisitions and the client’s read as one list. The queue says which firm it is counting.
  8. OPEN, FOUNDER 2026-09-21 — expertise margin made visible to the client. Addendum D distinguishes arbitrage margin from expertise margin and Requirement.margin_class carries it, but nothing shows a client that a supplier’s price is expertise: certifications its people hold, their tenure, outcomes on prior placements, beside the rate. The founder: “we need to help, push and enable suppliers towards that path.” The record enables and never pushes; this panel is the lever that does not exist yet. Sequenced after the document loop (L3.2.3.8).

L3.1.1.3Supplier release
10 tasks
  1. Choose who sees it
  2. Stagger by tier
  3. Set the response window
  4. A prime’s candidates arrive on the role the client released to it — including one it sends on from its own sub-vendor — never on a copy written onto the client’s books (FIXED 2026-09-28, break #3: "Send on" wrote a new requirement at the client every time, so the prime’s candidate never reached the requisition while a sub-vendor submitting direct did)
  5. Where the client released several roles to the prime and nothing on the prime’s record says which, the prime is asked which by title rather than guessed for; a role the client never released to it cannot be named into
  6. A candidate sent on meets the client’s own door: open, not paused, and first in wins — the same person already put forward by another firm is refused, not duplicated
  7. A prime puts forward somebody a supplier on its network offered it — a marketing-tier listing the consultant granted that supplier — straight onto the role the client released to it (FIXED 2026-09-28, break #4: the submit door read only a listing the prime itself held and refused with “the consultant must grant a listing first”, and the picker never offered the network at all, so the only road was the sub-vendor going round its prime to the client)
  8. The supplier’s consent and walls still decide: a retained listing is no offer, an ungranted or withdrawn one is none, ask-first is asked by the supplier, the client’s block and every hold stand, and the supplier’s own do-not-return list is never read out to the prime
  9. The rung below is written with it — the supplier to the prime at the rate the prime says it pays, on the prime’s own record of the role, already sent on — so the award buys from the supplier and never from the prime’s payroll; the supplier is told the rate, and the client reads the prime’s name and nothing under it
  10. Both kinds are computed from who holds the person and first in wins on both rungs

16 tasks
  1. Rules filter first

  4. The row says whether a model or arithmetic scored it, read from the agent-run ledger and never inferred from the basis sentence
  5. FIXED 2026-09-26: the Training page reported “Bench consultants 0 with skills listed” over Techpeple’s five fully skilled people, and computed its skill gap from that nought against a real demand side — so every skill a client asked for read as an unfilled deficit, on every supplier, for the life of the screen. It read the bench answer under `data.listings`, a key `/api/bench` has never sent; a missing key is undefined, `undefined ?? []` is `[]`, and `[]` counts to nought without complaining. `readBench` in lib/bench-filter is the one door now, and it refuses a shape it does not understand rather than returning a confident zero.
  6. FIXED 2026-09-26: a gap needs both sides, or neither. `skillGap` in lib/training returns null for skills-tracked and skills-short where the people side cannot be read, and where a firm has people but no skills on record at all — five engineers nobody can describe is a gap in the record, not in the bench, and the screen says so instead of sending a recruiter to buy training. Skills tracked used to be the union of the two maps, which on a broken supply side was the demand side wearing a name claiming to span both.
  7. FIXED 2026-09-26: the supply side counts the firm’s own payroll as well as its listings, once per person, so an integrator’s skill gap is computed over the people it actually employs. The course-enrollment picker had the same `data.listings` bug and offered nobody at every firm in the product’s life.
  8. FIXED 2026-09-26: the bench burn panel read “12 open reqs for matching” at a firm that could see one — `api/bench/burn` counted every OPEN requirement on the platform with no company filter, which is both a wrong number and a cross-tenant count. It reads `requirementScope`, the same rule the Requirements list itself uses.
  9. A sweep holds it: no screen that fetches /api/bench may read the answer’s own shape, and the five that still do are named in the test with their owner and what each one leaks — two of them (compliance, documents) have the identical picker bug and belong to etyme-regulatory
  10. BUILT 2026-09-30, the founder’s “bench is our wow factor”: matching brings bench to every job request, not only the raiser’s own. The pool is four circles, each by a consent the person gave (`lib/match-pool`): the viewer’s own listings and — for a firm that sells — its own employees between projects or coming off one within a month, who go forward as INTERNAL; the marketed bench of the firms it buys from; of the other firms it trades with; and, for a client on its own job request only, people who said yes to being shown in matches beyond their firm’s partners. Ranked in that order, then by score, and every row keeps factors, basis, confidence and unknowns
  11. BUILT 2026-09-30: a supplier the job request was sent to runs matching on it with its own pool, with no copy of the role; its suppliers’ people reach it only through its register, the same door the submission goes through. A refresh recomputes only the viewer’s own pool, rewriting rows in place so a match keeps its id
  12. BUILT 2026-09-30: every row has one action, chosen by the server so the screen cannot draw a button the door refuses. A firm that sells adds the person to the application through `/api/submissions` with its own firm and a real rate — its listing’s, what it last billed its own employee at, or one it types; a supplier’s person goes forward in its name, bought from the supplier at the supplier’s own rate. The placeholder rate and firm the page used to send are gone. A client asks the firm to put the person forward, on the thread for the job, and through the prime where the firm works under one
  13. BUILT 2026-09-30: a client never reads a rate off a match, and a rate factor says whether it fits, never the number. Every match shown writes a MATCH_VIEW access row per person, suggestions included, before the answer leaves
  14. FIXED 2026-09-30, bench tester: a prime putting a supplier’s person forward is asked two prices — what the supplier charges, prefilled from its listing, and what it bills — where one box sent payRate:null to a door that refused it (`submitFields`); somebody placed and billing past the job’s start is no longer offered, somebody rolling off before it is offered from the day after (`freeForJob`), and the availability reason reads the same free date as the row
  15. FIXED 2026-10-01, bench tester round two: one door decides who is free (`whenFree` in lib/bench-filter), read off every papered or running line at any firm — the bench rows, the matches and the training page all read it, so a person placed at a client reads “On a placement until” and never “Shown to our partners, free”, and somebody on a bench they agreed to with nothing running is free now. A partner’s bench never sends a person’s email; their skills stand in for a missing headline. A client is refused a bench at the route and on the page, in a sentence pointing to matching. A suggestion that outscores a supplier’s person says why it sits below
  16. BUILT 2026-10-06 (etyme-supply, f544add82): “What we need” sits at the top of Partner bench — skills, places, rate range and the receiving desk — and is read on Our bench by firms that already trade with the firm, one rung at a time. L3.1.2.5A suggestion from matching opens supplier onboarding
8 tasks
  1. A suggestion shows the firm, the skills, when the person is free and why they fit — never the person’s name, contact, headline, place or rate, and no handle to reach them by. It cannot be submitted or asked for
  2. A person appears as a suggestion only where they said yes to it, from their own page or the bench invitation (`BenchListing.showInMatches`, off by default), and never through a firm that sits below one of the client’s primes on a chain at the client, whatever they said
  3. Its one action is “Ask to add this firm”: a supplier request linked to the job request and the match, saying how the firm comes in — as a prime vendor, under the client’s program office (which may be Etyme’s own), or as a sub-vendor under one of the client’s primes. Etyme is never a prime vendor
  4. The request walks the same four desks as any recommendation, from the same first one (`lib/supplier-recommend`); the firm’s owner gets the link and its address is not written where the client’s desks read it
  5. Approval joins the firm already on Etyme rather than making a second company from its name. Under a prime, no agreement is written between client and sub — the paper is the prime’s — and the ask for its person goes to the prime
  6. Once approved the suggestion is an ordinary match, the person’s name shows, and the client can ask for them; their consent rules still apply
  7. Asking is for the desks that recommend suppliers; anybody else is refused in a sentence
  8. OPEN: the prime is not yet told that its client approved a sub-vendor to work under it, and nothing writes the prime’s own register row for the sub; that is the prime’s deal to paper

L3.1.2.7An integrator’s own people move between its projects
12 tasks
  1. The manager of a project flags one of the firm’s own employees “rolls off on” a day inside their placement, from the project team on Our bench; a day after the contract ends is refused as an extension, an earlier day is allowed and said, and the contract itself is not shortened. Only a manager of that project flags it (`managesLine`: the seat on the delivery unit or above it, or naming the person as team; a line naming no unit falls back to any manager, never refuses)
  2. A manager may keep somebody — “staying with me until” — and they read as free from that date, on Our bench and in matching
  3. Our bench (Bench → Our bench · employed) lists the firm’s own people rolling off or between projects with skills, place, free date, current project and the releasing manager; read by the firm’s managers and HR only, refused to every client and to an engineer on the roster in a sentence, the current project named only where the reader’s account wall allows, and every person shown on the access trail
  4. Ask about a person opens one thread per person inside the firm with the releasing manager, who is put on it and told (lib/threads: a firm’s own thread, no other company on it)
  5. A manager reserves a person for his own project’s order or, where his desk may submit, a client’s job request; one hold at a time, held in the database (`ProjectHold.live` unique per person), and a second is refused naming who holds them, for what, and until when. Two weeks by default, thirty days at most; the releasing manager keeps with a date and never holds; a hold is let go by its holder or the releasing manager; a lapsed hold is read off its date
  6. The releasing manager confirms the day; nobody flagged is placed before it. The holder places: (a) on a client’s job request through POST /api/submissions, where the employee goes forward as INTERNAL; or (b) a new sell line and W2 buy line on his own project’s existing order, on the order’s terms (`nextLineOnSameDocument`), the order line’s bill rate and the pay the person is on today unless the manager types others, DRAFT with its cycles as the award writes a line, starting the day after the old line ends or on the free date, never overlapping; the old placement’s end is untouched
  7. HR is told of every flag, hold, release, confirmation and move by email and in the app, and approves none of them; every step writes an attributed automation row naming who told whom
  8. The person is told at each step, never asked, by email and on their own page under “Your next project”; a move to another city says “This moves you from Portland to San Jose.”
  9. Matching (`lib/match-pool`) reads the flag over the contract: a flagged employee free within thirty days counts, somebody kept counts from their free date, and somebody already placed onto their next project is not offered again
  10. DECIDED 2026-09-30 by the founder: a delivery manager puts the firm’s own employee forward on a client’s job request, as INTERNAL; somebody the firm does not employ is refused in a sentence naming the recruiting desk (src/app/api/submissions/route.ts)
  11. OPEN: skills for an integrator’s employees come from a consultant profile nobody seeds for them, so the seeded Teleworld people read their seat’s discipline and “no skills on record”, and matching cannot weigh them until somebody records skills
  12. FIXED 2026-10-01, bench tester: a hold with no date reaches the day the person is free where that is later than two weeks, and a hold asked to end sooner says it lapses first (`checkHold`); keeping somebody past their contract’s end names the days with no contract under them (`keptPastContract`); a resold copy of a job request is not listed beside the one the firm was sent (`onePerJob`); a person put forward reads the client where the client belongs (`jobOnly`)

How far a listing reaches is read from two facts owned by two people (`whoSees` in lib/shared-consultant): the consent is the consultant’s and nothing reaches past the firm that asked until it is granted; the tier is the firm’s — retained keeps them to the firm, marketing shows them to the firms on its register.   15.   16. The timesheets door already admitted the person; the page never asked it. Your work now offers File your hours: the weeks still open, Monday to Sunday, trimmed to days that have happened, that the placement covers and that no filed sheet claims, and Send for approval writes the week through the timesheets door and sends it
  18.   19. BUILT 2026-09-29, founder (“who owes what, and when”): every week on the worker’s own page is in one of four places, said in plain words — sent and waiting for the client to sign it; signed and waiting for her employer (or, in a chain, each firm between) to accept it; owed to her; or paid. Only the last two carry money: a week the client signed and her employer has not accepted is never counted or shown as owed. Owed is what payroll pays for the hours her employer accepted, priced with payroll’s own call (`sheetPay` in lib/money/sheet-overtime), so a cut week is priced on the hours accepted and a week accepted at or under forty is straight time; each owed week carries the pay day it falls due on, read off her own pay line’s SALARY_PAY dates — the first on or after both the week’s end and the acceptance, whether or not payroll ran that day — and says “has not set a pay date for this week” where the line has none, rather than inventing one. A paid week shows what was paid and the day, read off the run that paid it. The page says what is owed, and how much of it is past its pay day, on one line, and what is still waiting on another with hours and no figure; no bill rate is on it (`owedByWeek`, `waitingWeek`, `weekSigners`, `paidDatesFrom`)

The page now reads the line’s pay periods and straddle through the same door payroll does (`periodTermsFor('BUY', …)`, then `hoursInPeriod`), shows each part of a crossing week with its own days, hours, amount and pay day, and shows one date where the line pays a crossing week whole.   31. L3.1.3.3Award and seat close
34 tasks
  1. Governance checks
  2. Seat arithmetic
  3. Raise both sides of the deal
  4. Stand down the rest
  5. Raise the purchase order with the contract as its first line, in one transaction — one open order per buyer and seller, found rather than raised twice
  6. The ceiling is what the requisition was approved at, carrying the basis it came from; where nothing supports a figure no order is raised and the answer says why
  7. A sub-vendor’s line hangs on the prime’s own order to the sub, and an employee’s line hangs on no order at all
  8. One road to placed: PLACED is written by the award and by nothing else, and a bare status change to placed is refused in a sentence that points the buyer at Place (FIXED 2026-09-28, B0 — a new consultant stopped at OFFERED because the flip people used wrote no contract)
  9. Place is offered wherever the buyer sees the candidate — the Submissions row and the requisition page — and only where the award would accept it, because the lists and the route ask the same function
  10. A supplier never awards its own candidate; somebody turned down, withdrawn or stood down is out of the running; a row marked placed with no contract behind it is repaired by the award rather than stranded
  11. DECIDED 2026-09-28: no offer-acceptance step between the offer and the award. Nothing in the BRD, the user stories or Addendum E asks for one — the rate is agreed at submission (JR-03) and the supplier is told of the offer — so none was invented
  12. The person placed is told, by email, where and through which firm — the one nearest them, who will call about the start — and no rate; only the top of a chain tells them, so a prime settling with its sub-vendor first announces nothing the client has not decided (FIXED 2026-09-28: the award told the raiser and the supplier’s desks and never the consultant)
  13. Standing down calls off the interviews the award makes pointless, in the award’s own transaction: the placed person’s open rounds always, every other open round once the job is filled; each party in each round is told on their own channel in one sentence, and the award’s record names the rounds (FIXED 2026-10-03, client tester s3-11: two turned-down candidates were still booked)
  14. A candidate stood down carries a reason code, TIMING — beaten to it, which never counts against the supplier’s bar — never a bare status
  15. The award answers in one paragraph, each thing once and in words: who is placed, how many others were told, how many rounds were called off, and any note — never "1 note(s)" or a note printed twice (FIXED 2026-10-03, s3-9)
  16. A filled job request says it is filled and by whom at the rate the award agreed, and offers neither Send to suppliers nor matches again (FIXED 2026-10-03, s3-10)
  17. FIXED 2026-10-06, the client tester’s leftovers: “Yours today” draws the same list the headline counts — every decision, every start paperwork will refuse, every supplier on site with no agreement — so the number at the top is the number of rows (`deskItems`); the On site tile says it counts people working today and how many more are signed; a filled job says “Filled by Daniel Okafor at $132/hr on Oct 26, 2026” and draws neither the Send to suppliers box nor the suppliers-working count; the overtime terms name time off only where the dialog offers it, and the week is named by its Sunday; Submissions filters use the row’s own status words
  18. FIXED 2026-10-06, second pass: turning a candidate down from the row calls off their open rounds (conversation’s `cancelRoundsFor`) and names them on the decision’s log row; the award refuses a line booked past the end client’s time limit in a sentence naming the date, a WARN taking a reason kept on its record (`endsPastLimit`); the headline counts every held start, not the first five; a person’s page says when a live contract runs past the limit (`runsPastSentence`); the approval panel says the over-the-limit sentence once in either wording; the Submit dialog offers each job once (`onePerJob`) and only people this firm has staffed; a match’s chip says “Moderate confidence · 1 not known”, with no count where the unknowns are sentences
  19. FIXED 2026-10-06 (outside chain audit 2026-10-05, section 6): the award writes no employment the person never agreed. Hop 0 — the person and the first firm — is written by the award only for an employee of that firm at the pay they are on today; for anybody else no pay line is written at any rate, and the placement reads “Awarded, terms pending”. Every hop above takes its rate from the submission that went up it, and a submission with no rate writes no $0 line either (`buySide`)

The agreement is a “Terms of engagement” paper on the pay line, countersigned by the firm and signed by the person. Employed by another firm is refused with the road that works: the employer puts them forward itself (`lib/award/hire-terms`, `app/api/submissions/[id]/terms`)
  21. The buyer cannot set what the seller pays below it: a pay rate on the award is refused in a sentence rather than written as the seller’s cost
  22. A start date before the award is refused unless the awarder ticks that the work is already under way and says why; the reason is kept on the award’s record. With no date typed, a needed-by day already gone becomes today. No cycle is written for a period that ended before the award, even where the work was under way, and the terms page writes no pay date already gone either (`noDatesBefore`)
  23. One placement, one word, on every screen: Awarded, terms pending · Papers pending · Ready to start · On site · Ended, from one function (`lib/award/placement-status`) read by the award, the terms page, the contractor register and the program page — the register no longer says “On site here. Nothing needs you.” about somebody who has not started

Nothing said about pay writes no pay line, and the start waits on the firm. The person is not asked on this door: a recorded placement has no submission and so no terms page, and a paper waiting on a signature nobody can give would hold the start for ever — a desk-written line with a rate is on record by `hopZero`’s own rule. Papering the deal, clearing the person, getting them on site. Onboarding lives here — five times.

L2.2.1 · Commercial papering — etyme-demand

CodeProcessStatusOwnerFilesTests
L3.2.1.1Agreement and SOW — the legal umbrella
15 tasks
  1. Terms, margin floor, payment days — warns with a reason code, never blocks
  2. A statement of work cannot be signed before anybody wrote what the work is
  3. A client reading the same agreement never sees the vendor’s floor
  4. Payment days say what they run from — receipt of the invoice, the invoice date, the end of the work period or approval — and an agreement written before anybody asked keeps counting from the period end
  5. An early-payment discount is as many rungs as were agreed, each a number of days and a rate, and an order may override the agreement’s
  6. An agreement has a term: the day it starts, the day it runs out, and whether it rolls on, renews itself or simply stops — and one nobody gave a term says so rather than looking like it runs forever
  7. An agreement has a standing that can be ended, with a reason, so its capacity and its margin floor stop enforcing when somebody tears it up
  8. A signature is a named person with a title on a named side, and an agreement is executed only when both sides have signed — one signature says which side still owes a counter-signature
  9. The executed document is a file on the record with a hash, not an attachment in somebody’s email — recorded and attested, never verified by us and never sent for e-signature
  10. Every change writes what the terms were before it, who made it and why, so “what were the payment days on 3 March” has an answer
  11. Only the desk that owns prices may change payment days, the margin floor or the term, and the refusal says who to ask
  12. The nightly job marks an agreement running out or run out, rolls the ones whose own paper says they renew, and tells the contracting desk at ninety, sixty and thirty days and once when it has lapsed
  13. An agreement is the umbrella and nothing more — a client that sends one order and one contractor is never made to paper one first: `Engagement.msaId` is optional, no route invents an agreement, and an invoice says who it is between through the order and the lines billed on it
  14. NOT YET: nothing records an agreement two firms actually negotiated. `api/clients`, `api/suppliers` and `api/supplier-requests/[id]` write an unsigned stub with thirty-day terms so a counterparty has a row, and `api/program/agreements` only reads, signs, amends and ends what is already there — so a term, payment days, a margin floor and the sub-vendor disclosure clause can be agreed at signing and typed in nowhere
  15. A screen says “agreement” or “MSA” and never prefixes it with “master” — that word belongs to the profitability roll-up, and two things that sound like one are two things nobody can tell apart

L3.2.1.4The work order — one row, named per viewer
13 tasks
  1. A client raises a purchase order; the supplier reads the same row as its sales order; the trade calls it a work order
  2. Issue to the sub-vendor
  3. Draw down and stop at the ceiling
  4. The ceiling, the four parties, the billing basis and its milestones on one row — an order carries a ceiling, a contract carries a rate
  5. Whether an unanswered timesheet counts as approved, and after how many working days — the client’s own term, read by the nightly job
  6. One order, a contract for each person on it
  7. Both numbers kept: the buyer’s PO number and the seller’s own order reference
  8. A line on it is named by the person and the site — “Purchase order PO-4471, line 2 of 5” to the client, “Sales order SO-0913, line 2” to the supplier — and never by a contract id
  9. A placement shows the document it hangs on: the ceiling, what has been billed against it, and everybody else on the same paper
  10. The award raises it with its first line, so nobody has to remember to — and a second award between the same two firms joins it rather than opening another
  11. A line reads its billing rhythm and its payment days from the document it is on, and keeps its own dates, because an order is not a person

BUILT 2026-10-06 by etyme-architect: the firms an order may go to are the buyer’s suppliers, read from the same desk the order is written on — the client’s in a seat, the office’s own with ?books=own — and a blocked supplier is offered nowhere (GET /api/companies/suppliers, lib/suppliers-of). mayWriteOrder refuses, in a sentence, an order to a firm that is not one of the buyer’s suppliers or that the buyer blocked

  4. Four desks in order — the recommender’s department lead, Procurement, HR, Finance — each verifying its own items and no other’s, nobody deciding the firm they recommended and nobody sitting at two desks
  5. The firm supplies its side through a link of its own, with nothing to sign up for; what it sends is received, never verified, until a desk says so
  6. A certificate of good standing is asked for on the way in and verified by HR, the way its insurance is — the type ships with a consequence and until 2026-09-21 nothing anywhere requested one
  7. What this client’s own purchase orders require of a supplier is on the checklist too, read through lib/document-requirements and never a second hardcoded list, each item saying whose order asked — so a client that invented a hot floor induction asks the firm for it before it may trade
  8. An item the walk already asks for is not asked twice when an order asks for it as well, and an item a desk has verified stays verified when the order set is folded in again
  9. An agreement an order requires is the desk’s to paper and never insisted on at this point, because the agreement is written when the last desk says yes
  10. A certificate a desk verifies at supplier onboarding becomes a row on the firm’s own compliance record, with the two dates printed on it, so the desk that cleared it and the gate that reads it stop disagreeing — and a verdict with no dates is refused rather than filed with no expiry
  11. FIXED 2026-09-22: a desk that verifies a verdict no desk in Etyme renders — a background check, a drug screen, an employer’s own I-9 — is told nothing went on the compliance record and whose opinion it would take, beside the item and again at approval. The item stays on the checklist as the desk’s own note with the file the firm sent, and does not read as verified. The refusal was landing silently: the route surfaced a verdict only where it succeeded or wanted dates, so a desk marked a screening report verified, nothing was written, and it saw nothing at all.

A call skips every step already finished for this world at this deployment, runs the next ones until thirty seconds have passed, and answers done, next and remaining, so repeating POST /api/seed-world converges where eight calls in a row had timed out on production. A finished world costs two queries and writes nothing; a new deployment walks every step again. The contracts every step writes shift off the same holidays whichever call writes them, because the calendar is worked out in memory at the top of every call. No step makes more than about 320 queries on a fresh world or 215 walked again after a deploy — about fifteen seconds at that rate — and a step past 350 fails the build. And the seed writes the demo world and nothing else: the books, postings, invoice orders, payment run, CVs, holds, verification files, I-9 evidence and visa petitions each read the whole database before and now read the roster, or an address nobody can register, so a real firm’s books and a real person’s papers are never written by a seed

L3.2.2.9A counterparty that is not on the system
7 tasks
  1. A firm on the register that has not taken possession of itself — it can be named, sent a role and scored; it cannot sign in and the network cannot see it
  2. A client lists a supplier that is not here, and a supplier lists a client that is not here — the same door, both ways round
  3. A firm already here under its own domain is never copied; the refusal says to ask them instead
  4. A claimed firm may write an order naming a shell on either leg, including the leg where it is not the natural issuer — so a supplier can record the purchase order its client handed it
  5. A firm cannot name a company that is already here as its counterparty without them
  6. The row says which of the two parties typed it in
  7. Every row already points at the company id, so it is the claimant’s the instant they take possession

L3.2.2.10The company’s own calendar
11 tasks
  1. A company adds its own days off, or seeds a country’s public holidays for a year in one click
  2. A holiday marked for one country does not move another site’s dates
  3. Which way a date moves off a weekend or a holiday is the company’s to set — the working day before, the working day after, or left where it falls
  4. Asked once for hours, once for pay and once for billing, because a firm that pays on the Friday before still bills on the Monday after

L3.2.3.1Work authorization
6 tasks
  1. Visa class and expiry
  2. Petition and transfer events
  3. Blocks, never warns
  4. A petition from filing to running out
  5. FIXED 2026-09-26: a compliance officer can pick the person they are filing a petition for. The Visas tab’s picker read /api/bench’s answer under data.listings — a key that route has never sent — coalesced undefined to an empty array, and drew an empty dropdown, so nobody could be filed for at any firm on the platform for as long as the route has answered in its present shape. Nothing failed, because an empty list is a valid-looking answer and an officer who sees nobody concludes there is nobody. The population was wrong as well as unread: a BenchListing is a consultant consenting to be marketed and a firm files an H-1B for somebody it employs, so the picker now asks askTheBooks in lib/document-request — the listings through supply’s one door in lib/bench-filter, the firm’s own payroll beside them, one row per person, each name saying why it is on the list — and a side that will not read says so in a sentence rather than offering nobody. Every name offered is filed for in the integration walk, so a dropdown cannot offer a name the route refuses.
  6. OPEN, FOUND 2026-09-22 — nothing in production writes a Verification for a person. The company half has a door: the supplier onboarding desks record a firm’s insurance and good standing as they verify each item (api/supplier-requests/[id]). The person half has none — every I-9, background check, passport, green card and visa row in the system was written by a seed, while contract clearance, the two-greens gate at activation, the expiry watch and the client’s paperwork verdict all read that table. On a real tenant the person’s half is empty, so a gate that is meant to BLOCK passes everybody: there is nothing to have lapsed. Candidate green is the half that fails open, and it is the half a client is exposed by. The document loop (L3.2.3.8) gave a line what it requires; what is still missing is the door a compliance officer walks through to record that a document was seen, and by whom, on what date, from which edition. Until it exists, no deployment is production ready on work authorization however green the tests are.

L3.2.3.3Insurance and indemnity
10 tasks
  1. Certificate on file and in date
  2. A lapse blocks; an absence chases — which cover is required is the client’s rule
  3. Cover that has not begun blocks the same as cover that ran out — and a renewal filed early does not block the firm that filed it
  4. Every desk reads the day cover begins, not only the day it ends — the compliance page, the packet, the submission door, the outbound pack, the nightly chase and the placement thread
  5. The weeks between one policy ending and the next beginning are chased, and the supplier is asked for cover for them rather than told to renew what it has already sent
  6. A sub-vendor’s cover on a placement answers with a computed standing rather than the status somebody typed when they filed it — and the thread prints the computed word, in the compliance page’s own vocabulary, with the sentence on the hover
  7. The verdict on the firm below a supplier — whether it could put anybody forward today, and what to do where it could not — is on the placement thread, in the words the submission door computed
  8. A firm reads the cover of every supplier it is answerable for: the ones with people at its own sites, and the ones it pays on a chain — so a prime can see whether the sub-vendor it pays is insured without reading its client’s book
  9. FIXED 2026-09-22: the nightly chase raised its letter from the shipped annual list alone, so a buyer that wrote a certificate of good standing onto its own order had it refused at a start, chased by the finding, and never asked for. The letter now merges what the buyer’s lines require, through lib/document-request — the same door the packets route asks — and the automation log records which items came from the buyer’s orders and how many lines said so, so a desk can answer a supplier’s “why are you asking me for this”.
  10. FIXED 2026-09-22, found by the test above rather than by reading: the chase looked for the buyer above a supplier through the supplier’s own sell lines and a counterparty register, and a prime buying through a sub holds a buy line while the sub holds nothing of its own. Neither branch matched, so the chase concluded the sub had no buyer and sent the letter from the sub to the sub — “remind yourself” — while the prime that pays it, and whose placement a lapse stops, heard nothing. The buy line is now the third branch. Every seeded chain was in this state.

L3.2.3.6What kind of thing a document is
5 tasks
  1. Three purposes, and the purpose is the behavior — compliance is watched, an agreement is signed, proof stands behind something else
  2. Three validity shapes — never expires, runs out, covers a period — and the start of the period is read
  3. The list is the company’s: a type it invents behaves from the first document filed against it, with no migration
  4. A form has an edition, and an edition the issuer had already replaced is an audit finding rather than a bar to work
  5. A form is not evidence on its own — an I-9 records what somebody looked at, and what they looked at is recorded

L3.2.3.4Attestation of a check
18 tasks
  1. Records that a check happened, never a verdict
  2. Says no on statutory checks however fresh
  3. Counts how many firms hold a copy
  4. Asked for, sent, uploaded, signed
  5. FIXED 2026-09-26: a desk asking for a document can pick who to ask. “From whom” on the Paperwork page had the same bug as the Visas picker — data.listings, a key /api/bench has never sent, read as an empty list — so no document could be asked for from this screen at any firm. Both pickers now ask one door, askTheBooks in lib/document-request, which reads the listings through lib/bench-filter and the firm’s own payroll beside them: asking somebody for a W-9 or an NDA needs no consent to be marketed. Three states are kept apart on the screen and never collapsed into an empty dropdown — a side that would not read, a firm with nobody on its books yet, and a list shortened because half of it failed — and a desk that may not read people is shown the route’s own refusal.
  6. A worker sends the file itself and it is kept as the file — a photograph of an I-9 from a phone, not an address on a system she does not have. Nothing stored a document’s bytes until 2026-09-21, so a multipart POST arrived empty and the app told her she had sent nothing.
  7. A file too large, or of a kind whoever checks it could not open, is refused in words before anything is recorded — so a refusal never leaves a request saying a document arrived and a record with nothing in it. The size is checked again on what arrived, because a body can be larger than the header claimed.
  8. A link is still a way to answer, because a firm sending one from its own document system is not a contractor standing in a corridor with a photograph
  9. The request and the file move together or neither does, and one file per instance — a reissue is a new instance with its own file, so the edition somebody signed keeps the bytes they signed
  10. Two may open it and no third: the person it is about, and the firm that asked for it. Every read writes an AccessLog row, the refusals included, and a stranger is told the document is not here rather than that they may not read it — a refusal that confirms a document exists is a refusal that leaked something.
  11. A page withholds a sentence about a company until it knows the company’s name: the tenure page read “Cross-vendor tenure at … .” while the fetch was in flight, and an ellipsis in the middle of a sentence is not a loading state
  12. FIXED 2026-09-22: a worker is asked for her consent and never for the report. A background check was carried as a document she supplies — the same shape as a passport — so her own paperwork page listed it as hers, the nightly chase asked her for it, and POST /api/me/papers let her open a request against it. The provider posts the report to the firm that ordered it and to nobody else. What she owes is her permission and the details it is run against; the row on her page now says which firm orders it, offers her no upload and opens no request, and the refusal names that firm rather than telling her nobody is asking.
  13. FIXED 2026-09-22: a screen never reports a check as verified without the provider’s name on it. Verification.provider and referenceId have existed since the table did and nothing in production wrote either, so a row reading CLEAR was a screening company’s report or a desk clicking a button and no reader could tell which. readVerdict says “Sterling reported clear on 2026-03-12, reference 4471” where a name is on the row and “recorded here by Dana Whitfield — no screening company is named on it, so it is this firm’s own note” where none is. No verdict moves either way: a background check warns when it is missing, whoever ran the last one, because Addendum E says warn, capture a reason and proceed.
  14. FIXED 2026-09-22: no desk in Etyme renders a verdict a third party renders. The supplier walk turned any compliance item a desk marked verified into a Verification of CLEAR authored by whoever clicked it — exactly right for a certificate of insurance, where the insurer made the assertion and printed the two dates, and Etyme declaring a person clear to work for a background check or a drug screen. Which of the two a document is is now asked of lib/attestation rather than kept as a second list here, so a screening company’s verdict and an employer of record’s own statutory check are both refused, in a sentence that names the party whose opinion it is and says what a real record of it would carry — their name, their reference number and the day they ran it. The desk’s note and file stay on the checklist, which is the honest record of what the firm sent (src/lib/onboarding-evidence.ts).
  15. FIXED 2026-09-22, platform — a passport is no longer told that nothing about it expires. lib/attestation has recognized PASSPORT and DRIVERS_LICENSE as an IDENTITY check the employer of record renders since it was written, and lib/onboarding-evidence filtered every key through its own VERIFICATION_TYPE map before asking whose check it was — so a key with no enum row never reached regulation’s table at all and fell to the sentence for a screening a desk ran itself: “nothing here expires”, about a document with an expiry date printed on the front of it. Worse than a wrong sentence, because the supplier walk surfaces it: whoRendersItem reads the key directly, saw EMPLOYER, and printed this file’s wrong sentence beside its correct attention mark. Who renders a check is now asked of every type the item declares and the enum filter runs after, so the refusal names the employer of record. Three nothings that shared one sentence are now three: a check with no document type behind it expires nothing, a signed agreement lives with the agreement, and a type the compliance record has no column for says so and says somebody has to watch its expiry by hand. Reachable only on an item a client’s own order added, which is exactly the surface that is open by design (src/lib/onboarding-evidence.ts).
  16. OPEN, NOT BUILT — nothing in the app knows FCRA exists. The verdict transfers to the provider and the process around it does not: under US law the firm ordering a background check owns the consent and the disclosure before it, and the adverse action steps after an unfavorable result — the pre-adverse notice, a copy of the report, a waiting period, the final notice. There is no consent, no disclosure, no notice, no waiting period and no TODO anywhere in src. It is not being built now because nobody orders a check through Etyme today — no route, manual or API, sends a package to a provider — and the day one does, this is the step that generates the lawsuits rather than the one that gets skipped. Named here so it is refused deliberately rather than forgotten.
  17. OPEN — the copy count is arithmetic with nothing calling it. exposureOf says how many firms hold a copy of one person’s identity documents, and no route or screen asks it, so the third task on this row is a unit test rather than a number a privacy officer can read.
  18. DECIDED 2026-09-22, architect — a provider and a reference number are a check in the door and not a column, for now. Verification has carried provider and referenceId since it was written and nothing in production sets either, so a row reading CLEAR could be Sterling’s report or somebody clicking a button. The constraint that would fix it is conditional — not null only where the type is provider-rendered and the status is an answer — which Prisma cannot express and which would surface to a desk as a database error rather than a sentence. There is exactly one production writer of a CLEAR row and it is the one now refusing to write these at all, so the door is the whole surface. readVerdict already refuses to dress a row up: where nobody is named it says nobody is named. When the step that orders a check from a provider is built, that is the second writer, and the column constraint goes in underneath it with the data already conforming. Regulation asked the same morning for something different and it is granted: Verification.orderedByCompanyId and orderedAt, with an index, because companyId is the subject of a company-level check and is null on a person’s, so no row could name the firm that bought the report. mayRelyOn says a background check is point in time and that passing on somebody else’s report is a regulated act of its own; it is exported, correct, and had nothing to feed it, so the reliance rule is not built rather than built on a guess — a refusal on a guess blocks the wrong people. NOT BUILT, and said rather than implied: no production route writes either column, because nothing in Etyme orders a check from a provider yet. The seeds write them where the demo world knows who bought the report, null means nobody recorded it and never “we ordered it”, and adding a column is not building a feature.

8 tasks

  3. A license in date today that runs out inside the assignment warns with the days counted rather than refusing work the law permits

  7. The nightly chase asks the person sixty days ahead, through the firm that places them, with the board named and the link theirs
  8. A license already renewed is not asked for twice, and the ask on a seeded seat is one the chase raised rather than one the seed typed

L3.2.3.8The document loop between parties
50 tasks
  1. A line says what it requires on paper, and every item says which party owes it — the worker, the supplier, the customer, or us
  2. A line with no set of its own inherits the set on the order above it; a line on no order falls back to the default for its shape
  3. A line may override one item, and the override says who changed it and why
  4. A client asks for a document it invented itself — a hot floor induction, a sterile field training — and it reaches the line with no migration
  5. The default set is a floor: an order adds to it and nobody orders their way out of a federal form
  6. A waived item stays on the list, marked, with the reason and the name of whoever waived it — never deleted
  7. Work authorization cannot be waived, and a waiver already on the row is refused rather than honored quietly
  8. A signed paper carries dates, an edition and a countersignature, so an NDA can be watched the way a certificate is
  9. A certificate of good standing stops a supplier the way lapsed cover does
  10. The required set is computed and never materialized, so a default that changes is not frozen into rows written last month
  11. A firm is asked for its certificate of good standing on the way in, and HR verifies it before the firm may trade
  12. A firm recommended to a client whose orders require a document is asked for that document too, on its own page, and every such item says whose order asked
  13. An agreement running out is told to both firms that signed it, each in its own words — the supplier reads a renewal to start, the client reads how many people are on its sites under it
  14. An agreement between a prime and its sub-vendor is told to those two firms and never to the client above them
  15. A supplier’s row on the register names the documents this client’s orders require of it and it cannot be shown to hold; what nothing here could evidence is counted, never reported as missing
  16. A start resolves against the line’s own set rather than a packet picked off the role, and the refusal names whose order asked for the item
  17. A waived item stays on the checklist and never blocks, with the reason and the name in the verdict; a waiver against work authorization is refused and no row is written
  18. A lapsed certificate of good standing blocks a start and a submission; one nobody ever asked for is not a lapse and says nothing
  19. A client’s program manager or compliance officer changes what its own order asks for; a supplier may read it and not change it
  20. A worker’s own page shows every document on her file with the day it runs out, months before any chase fires
  21. A document she has already sent is not asked for again the next morning — it reads as sent and waiting, asks her to do nothing, and still counts as nothing on file, because a check still running is not a document
  22. A permanent resident is not chased for proof of her right to work while holding a green card, an employment authorization document or a completed I-9; a passport is not taken as that proof, because a foreign passport proves identity and nothing more
  23. A firm that has filed nothing reads “nothing on file” rather than a clear rate of a hundred percent over no checks, and its own compliance page lists what it owes on the lines it is paid on — read through the one door, so its page and its customer’s dashboard name the same documents

  31. A certificate a desk verifies at supplier onboarding becomes a row on the firm’s own compliance record, with the two dates printed on it, so the desk that cleared it and the gate that reads it stop disagreeing — and a verdict with no dates is refused rather than filed with no expiry

OPEN, ARCHITECT — two relations between documents point in opposite directions and one list cannot hold both. backedByAnyOf means what must stand behind this and makes an item weaker: a held I-9 with nothing behind it is not held. Between the same two keys the edges reverse — an I-9 is backed by right to work, and right to work is satisfied by an I-9. The answer is a sibling field, satisfiedByAnyOf, on the spec and on the row, so a client can declare its own equivalence; it is not built, because no client has asked and CLAUDE.md says add the setting the first time a paying client needs it.   6. A week this side has already signed reads as signed, names who it is waiting on, offers no second tick and leaves this side’s count

  8. DECIDED 2026-09-30 by the founder, “A client may approve by email, and the proof travels down the chain”. RULES BUILT, by demand (src/app/api/timesheets/approval-by-email.ts): a one-time link to the client’s approver runs out after seven days — the widest approval window a company may set — and is refused in a sentence once it approved, once it sent the week back, once the client approved another way, once the week was sent again, or once it ran out; sending back takes a reason from a closed list; evidence (the approval email, a PDF, or an export from the client’s own system) is refused without the approver’s name and address, or dated before the week ended; only the worker on her own week or the timesheet desk at a supplier on the chain sends a link or attaches evidence, and the client’s own desk is told to approve in Etyme; it applies to every contract on the chain unless fewer are picked, always including the client’s own; every rung it applies to reads the evidence and only its own contracts in it, so a client never learns a sub-vendor’s contract, and every read is an access log row, refusals included; a week approved this way reads “Approved by email: Dana Whitfield, Oct 2 — evidence attached”, never that the client signed in Etyme; it writes the client’s signature only and every rung below still accepts in turn
  9. BUILT 2026-10-01 by the architect, end to end. Schema: WeekApproval (the timesheet, LINK or EVIDENCE, the client, the approver’s name and address, who sent or attached it and as which, a hashed one-time token with sent, expires and used times, the outcome and its reason code, the evidence kind and the day approved, and the CLIENT_APPROVAL assertion it wrote), WeekApprovalContract (the contracts it applies to, top first) and WeekApprovalFile (the evidence bytes, read only when opened). The worker on her own week or a supplier’s timesheet desk sends “Approve by email” or attaches evidence from the week’s own page (/dashboard/weeks/[id]), picking the contracts, all by default; the letter leaves through the email path and the send is an automation log row. The approver opens /answer/week/[token] with no account and presses Approve or Send back with a reason; every open is an access log row; a used, sent-back, expired, overtaken or already-approved link is refused in a sentence. Approving writes the client’s signature only — a CLIENT_APPROVAL naming nobody, at the client’s own rate — and the next rung is told and accepts in its turn through the approve route, as before. A flagged week, hours over the client’s overtime line, and a client that employs the worker itself are refused by email and signed in Etyme. Every rung it applies to reads “Approved by email: <name>, <day> — evidence attached” and opens the evidence, each read logged, refusals included, its own contracts only; a sender from a firm below the client’s supplier is never named to the client, in the letter, on the link page or on the week.   12. OPEN 2026-10-03, for the founder: evidence is served to every rung it applies to as the bytes that were attached, and only the metadata is masked. L3.3.2.2Employer acceptance
9 tasks
  1. Accepts the basis for pay
  2. A different number needs a reason
  3. DECIDED 2026-09-28 by the founder: the signed week travels down the chain — the client signs first, then each firm down the chain accepts what it pays, the employer last; no rung accepts before the rung above it has, and every rung accepts the one week, never a copy
  4. FIXED 2026-09-28: the firm in the middle had no step — Computer Systems, which pays Techpeple for every hour of Helena Marsh’s week, was refused as “not the company that pays this person”. It now accepts in its turn as PASS_THROUGH on the ledger, the role built for it and never written
  5. FIXED 2026-09-28: the employer could accept before the client had signed. A firm whose turn has not come is told who it is waiting on, and the timesheet list and the decisions queue offer the week to a firm only in its turn
  6. Each rung is told when the week reaches it — on its desk and by email — naming who signed above it and whom it pays, never a rate
  7. FIXED 2026-09-28 by etyme-money (2bfd3a931): a firm pays its supplier’s invoice against its own acceptance. The invoice-receipt match read only EMPLOYER_ACCEPTANCE, and only on a contract linked to the payer’s buy contract, which in a chain carries no hours — so Techpeple’s invoice to Computer Systems matched nothing whoever had signed. It now reads the payer’s own signature: EMPLOYER_ACCEPTANCE where it carries the hours itself, PASS_THROUGH where they are filed on a supplier’s contract below it, and a week the payer has not accepted is counted as waiting, never priced from another firm’s signature
  8. BUILT 2026-10-01 with approve-by-email (L3.3.2.1): a week the client approved by email, by link or by evidence, is a client signature like any other, so each rung below accepts it in its turn — Computer Systems as PASS_THROUGH, then Techpeple as the employer — and nobody accepts for another; the evidence attached is opened by every rung it applies to, each read logged
  9. FIXED 2026-09-28: the seeded programs and the world under them signed a chain week with the client and the employer only, and the programs dated the employer the day before the client. Every signed seeded week now carries the client, then each firm in the middle as PASS_THROUGH at the rate it pays, then the employer, in that order, so the seeded prime-to-sub invoices have a receipt of the prime’s own behind them. And no seeded signature is made by somebody who does not work at the firm that signs: the world’s one firm nobody has joined (Bluecrest) used to accept its weeks through a person at Pinnacle; it is now off the chain, and Pinnacle carries the hours on its own contract and accepts what it pays, the product’s path for a supplier that is not on the platform

L3.4.1.1Bill generation
22 tasks
  1. BUILT 2026-09-30 by etyme-money, handed over by demand: a bill prices a week against the line it was decided on — the contract’s own, else the job’s hours where somebody decided the week (lineFor) — in generation and in the three-way check alike, so a premium chosen on a 45-hour week of a 40-hour job reaches the bill
  2. BUILT 2026-09-30 by etyme-money, from a tester’s walk as Techpeple: a bill never covers hours already on a bill to the same firm, however that bill was made. Generation reads the invoice receipts the payer recorded from this firm as well as its own bill lines; a week inside one is left off with a sentence naming the receipt, and a week partly inside one is left off whole rather than split by a guess (lib/money/billed-elsewhere). Recording an invoice receipt over hours a generated bill already holds is refused the same way, and nobody may wave either through
  3. From approvals, not a rate card
  4. Cycle, straddle and holiday calendar
  5. A week over the line bills what whoever signed it decided — never what the contract offered
  6. An hour nobody has decided is not billed at any price, and the invoice says how many it left off
  7. A decision that has reached an invoice is stamped billed, and billed cannot be changed
  8. A line prints the working that adds up to it, and never a multiplication that does not come out
  9. The due date counts from what the contract says it counts from, so an invoice raised six days after the period ends is not claimed overdue six days early
  10. The day the client received it is recorded, because that is the day a net-30 clock actually starts, and a due date anchored on a receipt nobody confirmed says so rather than guessing
  11. Nothing schedules a due date in advance: the invoice carries its own, so no second answer is generated on the calendar to disagree with it
  12. The day a bill is to be raised is put in front of accounts receivable a week out, in their own words, and never in front of the contractor it is about
  13. The picker offers only what the gate will accept: one function over one cascade decides both which engagements are listed and which are refused, and a firm with nothing to bill is told why rather than handed a box asking for a database id
  14. FIXED 2026-09-22: a cycle date is the end of a period, and the shipped packs asked for two that were not. The semimonthly cut said the 1st, which matches no period end lib/periods defines — it asked for an invoice on the first day of the half-month it would bill, a fortnight before those hours existed, and the 1st-to-15th period was never closed: 20 dates a year with gaps of 1, 3 and 32 days where the 15th and month-end give 24 with gaps of 14 to 18. And the weekly timesheet approval was a Monday series anchored separately at the contract start, so a contract starting Saturday, Sunday or Monday got an approval four days before its first submission — never claimed by pickCycle, and called overdue on the placement timeline for the life of the contract. It is three days after the hours are due, said with offsetDays, which also gives the last week of a contract the approval date a Monday-anchored series stopped short of. Diagnosed with numbers by etyme-money in lib/cycle-generator, changed in lib/template-packs by etyme-regulatory, and the UK pack carried the identical approval line and was changed with it. On a world seeded afterwards: 0 of 916 adjacent invoice and vendor-bill cycle pairs land within two days of each other, and 0 of 32 placements with hours cycles have an approval before a submission.
  15. FIXED 2026-09-26: the same defect one frequency up, in the two packs that bill monthly. IN_DELIVERY and UK asked for their invoice, their supplier invoice and India’s monthly timesheet approval on dayOfMonth: 1 — the first day of the month a cycle date is supposed to close, so every date fell inside the month it would bill, thirty days early. Measured against lib/periods’ calendarMonth rather than asserted: on a twelve-month contract through 2026, none of the twelve invoice dates was at or after the end of the month it was paired with, the first (1 January) billed nothing, and December was closed by no cycle at all. Worse on the vendor side, because VENDOR_BILL_GENERATE is a PAY kind and shifts BACKWARD off a weekend: six of twenty-four UK dates were recorded in the month before the work — 30 January 2026 for a February that had not begun. Repaired as month-end with offsetDays: 1, which keeps the coherent intent (“bill on the 1st for last month”) and every date from the second onward, drops the spurious head and gains the tail: 12 of 12 months now invoiced at or after they end, 0 of 24 vendor bills dated before the work. The monthly TIMESHEET_APPROVE is month-end with offsetDays: 3 — over 24 months from all 28 start days of the month, 672 submissions, shipped dayOfMonth: 1 gave 24 approvals before their paired submission, 1 start day in 28 with an inverted head, 1 in 28 whose last month could not be approved and 216 same-day collisions (32%); month-end +1 gave 0, 0, 0 and 224; month-end +3 gave 0, 0, 0 and 0. The three is the founder’s own answer, decided 2026-09-26 when he was asked whether a client should sign a month off the next day or three days later like the weekly packs: three days later, because it is the only variant where an approval never falls on the same calendar day the hours are due, which under the shipped dates happened a third of the time. And the relayed claim that IN_DELIVERY approved a month twenty-seven days early was FALSE — MEANS_MONTH_END is 28 — which is why both changes were re-derived before either was applied.
  16. FIXED 2026-09-26: nine hours of signed work billed to nobody, and the default was not the bug. __integration__/premium-invoice.test.ts went red on Omar Haddad’s week — Monday 31 August to Friday 4 September 2026, nine hours a day, 45 hours signed by Northbend Athletic’s hiring manager with five at time and a half. The September invoice billed 36 of them, $5,082 against $6,270, and SPLIT was right to say so: one day of that week belongs to August and hoursInPeriod flagged it partial with an honest note. Monday’s nine hours were then on no invoice, and none was coming. Two facts close that door and neither is a knob. InvoiceLine is unique on (timesheetId, sellContractId) — "one timesheet bills once, ever", the schema’s own words, because it is the whole anti-double-billing control and lives in the database rather than in a service — so the August days have no second line to go on. And generation runs forward, so a period behind an engagement’s first billing cycle is never raised: there is no August invoice on that engagement and there never will be. SPLIT is therefore exact arithmetic that cannot be written down. The relayed fix — move the shipped straddle default from SPLIT to END — was REFUSED: it would have made this one placement right and left every client who chose SPLIT losing the same hours, and SPLIT is a setting the product offers on purpose for a client that will not accept a part-week line. A defect made rarer is a defect made harder to find. It also could not have been done here, because seed-programmes writes billStraddle SPLIT on the header and that file is the architect’s. Resolved in lib/periods instead, where the arithmetic is: billingStraddle names what a bill can record, START and END are untouched because each puts the whole week in one period, and only SPLIT falls back — to END rather than START, because END never bills ahead of the work (a week beginning 29 September under START would bill four unworked days) and because hoursInPeriod has fallen back to END for a sheet with no daily breakdown since it was written, which is the same situation. The reason rides on the line rather than moving the hours quietly, and billableInPeriod is the one door, so the invoice route and the three-way match cannot reach two answers about one week. Measured on the seeded world rather than asserted: of 54 client-signed timesheets 1 crosses a calendar month end, carrying 9h and $1,188 stranded before the change and 0 after; of 42 billed timesheets, 0 are now billed for fewer hours than were signed. The second relayed fault was FALSE — the premium was not ridden whole onto the wrong slice. billableInPeriod judges the week whole and puts the over-hours on the day the week actually crossed the line, which was Friday, so the two halves came to 9 ordinary plus 31 ordinary plus 5 premium: exactly 45 hours, 40 at the usual rate and 5 at time and a half, adding up across the cut. The apportionment was the only thing about SPLIT that was already correct, and it was re-derived before anything was changed. One invariant sentence was replaced rather than relaxed — "a week straddling two months is judged whole and billed in the days that fall in each" asserted that between two invoices the week is billed once and in full, which is true of the arithmetic and false of the money because the second invoice cannot exist — and five sentences stand where it did, with the straddle pinned on fixed dates so it is tested on purpose rather than on the days lib/seed-days happens to produce. What would make SPLIT recordable is periodStart and periodEnd on InvoiceLine with the unique relaxed to (timesheetId, sellContractId, periodStart): a schema request for etyme-architect, and not urgent, because nothing is lost now.
  17. FIXED 2026-09-28 by etyme-money (12796ceee): a rung bills the hours the firm above it accepted, not the hours worked; a reduced week with overtime, crossing the bill’s edge, or partly accepted is left off in a sentence rather than guessed at
  18. FIXED 2026-10-03 by etyme-money, from a client tester’s walk: a bill refused for want of a signed week names the week, the person and who must sign first — “Omar Haddad’s week of Sep 21 is waiting for Northbend Athletic to sign it” — where it said “No approved timesheets left to bill” (lib/money/nothing-to-bill); a week not sent yet, sent back, or already on one of our bills says that instead. A due date reads “Oct 15, 2026”, never “2026-10-15”. A placement’s billing dates read to the client as an invoice receipt expected, never a bill to raise (labelOf with the reader in lib/cycle-kinds) — OPEN: app/api/placements/[id] is the architect’s and must pass its side to labelOf for the screen to change
  19. FIXED 2026-09-29 by etyme-money, on the founder’s rule 4: those three cases are now priced, not left off. The hours not accepted come off the hours over the overtime line first, then off ordinary hours, each walking from the last day backward, so where a week crosses a bill’s edge the later bill’s days are cut first; on one day the hours worked go before paid leave. A partial acceptance is priced on the days it covers, with the week still judged whole against the line. What is left over the line keeps the week’s own decision — premium billed, banked billed by nobody, undecided left off and said. The three-way check prices the line by the same call, so a bill made by the rule passes and a bill for the hours worked fails the hours check. Still left off in a sentence: more than one acceptance from the payer on one week, and more hours accepted than worked where the week has an overtime line, crosses a bill’s edge, or is only partly accepted
  20. BUILT 2026-10-06 by etyme-money: a cycle can be bounded by the day it is due as well as by the period it closes (`noneDueBefore` in `lib/cycle-generator`, passed through `writeCyclesFor`). An award for work already under way owes the reminder for a week that ended before it and falls due after it; bounding by the period dropped it. The extension keeps its period floor, because a period the first run settled must not be written again when a company has since changed its weekend direction
  21. FIXED 2026-10-06: the earliest reminder of its kind is not claimed by a period that ended a whole rhythm or more before it (pickCycle guard), tested in __tests__/invariants/cycle-complete.test.ts and __integration__/status-ledger.test.ts
  22. FIXED 2026-10-06 by etyme-regulatory (0ec3dcbf9): weekly hours are due the Monday after a Sunday-to-Saturday week and approved the Wednesday, said as Friday + 3 and + 5 because a Saturday anchor drops the last week of a Monday-to-Friday contract; biweekly pay falls the Friday after the fortnight and is calculated the Wednesday, on one anchor
