L3.5.1.1Payroll instruction
20 tasks
  1. Export to ADP, Paychex or a file
  2. From acceptance, never from a rate card
  3. A pay run that spans two currencies says both totals and never adds them into one; a figure a person reads is minor units through the one formatter, never a dollar sign typed in front of a column of cents — a placement at $145/hr was recorded in the diary as $14,500/hr until 2026-09-22
  4. OPEN, FOUNDER — a commission run adds an agent’s margin across their linked sell lines without reading each line’s currency, so an agent with placements in two currencies has rupees added to dollars before anything is formatted. That is a wrong number rather than a wrong symbol, and refusing or splitting the run changes what a commission run does: what a commission on a two-currency book even is, is a product question, not an arithmetic one
  5. Pay day reaches the payroll desk a week out — the nightly scan read only the sell leg and so had never once surfaced one
  6. BUILT 2026-09-29, founder (“yes to all”): a nonexempt US worker is paid overtime after 40 hours a week where neither the buy line nor the sell line draws one, because the law does — in the run, on the screen, on the file and in back pay, through one door (lib/money/pay-line). A line a contract drew stands, except that a line past 40 does not hold a nonexempt US worker past the law’s 40. An exempt worker keeps straight time; a worker nobody classified keeps straight time and the week over 40 says, in the existing words, that nobody has said whether they are exempt; work recorded under another country’s rules, or at a site, an entity or a currency outside the US, is not held to the US 40 and the week says why. The client’s bill does not move
  7. BUILT 2026-09-29, founder (“yes to all”): pay is the hours the employer accepted, never the hours filed, and where fewer are accepted the cut comes off ordinary hours first, from the latest day backward, so the worker keeps their overtime — the opposite of the bill’s cut, on purpose. One allocation for the run, the screen, the file and back pay (lib/money/pay-hours): 45 worked and 42 accepted on a 40-hour line pays 37 ordinary and 5 overtime, and 41 accepted pays 36 and 5
  8. BUILT 2026-09-29, founder: an acceptance at or under the line is the hours worked. Where the employer accepts 40 hours or fewer of a longer week — the line in force, the contract’s own or the law’s 40 — those hours are paid at straight time: 38 of 45 pays 38, 40 of 45 pays 40. The line is judged on hours worked, never on paid leave. The week says so on the payroll screen, in the run and as a note on the payroll file (“38 of 45 hours accepted; paid at straight time because the accepted week is not over 40.”); the file pays it rather than leaving it off, and back pay tops it up at straight time with no premium. sheetPay (lib/money/sheet-overtime) is the one call a worker’s page makes for a cut week. Replaces the hold the first version carried
  9. Every hour is paid at the rate in force on the day it was worked, and overtime in a week paid at two rates is priced on the US regular rate (29 CFR §778.115) by default
  10. The paying firm may choose another overtime method on the pay line — the rate on the day, or the higher rate — recorded with who chose it, when and why; anything but the default needs a reason, and only a desk that reads what people cost may change it. Founder, 2026-09-29
  11. Whatever is chosen, a nonexempt US worker is never paid less than the regular-rate premium, and the week says when the law’s figure was paid instead
  12. FIXED 2026-09-29 by etyme-money: the payroll file (src/app/api/payroll/export/route.ts) reads the overtime-method columns on the buy line, so it pays the method the run pays rather than the default
  13. BUILT 2026-09-30 by etyme-money, founder-approved for the seeded world only: a demo employer pays monthly — worked out at month-end + 4 and paid at month-end + 9, measured as the smallest pair where no pay day comes before its hours and the calculation is always two days ahead of pay after a weekend or holiday moves both back. writeCyclesFor takes it as an override (DEMO_MONTHLY_PAY in lib/contract-cycles) that moves only the two pay kinds and only on a payroll line; no pack ships it and only lib/seed-* and lib/demo-* may pass it. DONE 2026-09-30 by the architect: every seeded and demo payroll line passes it (lib/seed-doors, seed-world, seed-programmes, seed-rate-change, seed-sector-suppliers, demo-placement, demo-seed-consultant), and Karthik Menon’s placement is three whole months with a pay day for each
  14. BUILT 2026-09-30 by etyme-money, founder (“go with your recommendations, but keep settings user configurable”): a week accepted over the line is cut by the pay line’s own rule, read once by cutOvertimeFor. The default pays overtime only on the accepted hours above the line — 41 of 45 pays 40 + 1, 42 pays 40 + 2 — and a firm that keeps the week’s overtime, named and reasoned, is paid ordinary-first — 41 pays 36 + 5. The rule is a required argument in lib/money/pay-hours, so the run, its screen, the payroll file, back pay and the worker’s page cannot pay the default to a worker whose employer chose otherwise. At or under the line is straight time either way; the bill is not touched
  15. BUILT 2026-09-30 by etyme-money: a run marks done the pay days of the periods it pays, read off the line’s own pay days — a pay day belongs to the period holding most of the days since the one before it — rather than every date up to four days past the period, which missed a monthly pay day nine days after the month and settled the month before’s
  16. BUILT 2026-09-30, founder (“go with your recommendations, but keep settings user configurable”): each pay line carries how overtime is paid when fewer hours are accepted than were worked — “Only accepted hours over 40 (default, what the law requires)” or “Keep the week’s overtime (ordinary hours cut first)” — chosen on the placement’s pay line by the firm that pays, from a desk that reads what people cost; keeping the week’s overtime needs a reason, and the choice is recorded with who, when and why (PATCH /api/placements/:id/cut-overtime). Payroll reads it through one call, cutOvertimeFor in lib/cut-overtime-choice
  17. FIXED 2026-09-30 by etyme-money: payroll reads the cut-week setting — lib/money/pay-hours and sheetPay cut by cutOvertimeFor on every line (below). CLOSED 2026-09-30 by the architect: PAYROLL_READS_CUT_OVERTIME is true, and the pay line’s sentence names the rule payroll pays with no “not yet” clause
  18. BUILT 2026-09-30 by etyme-money: a week paid by a run is paid on the pay day the run settled, never the day the run was pressed — August read “paid on Sat, Sep 5” and a last day of August “paid Mon, Sep 7” (Labor Day) while the pay day was Wednesday 9 September. A run pressed after its pay day paid late, on the day it ran; a payment that settled no pay day was paid the day it was made (paidOnDay in lib/money/pay-day-period). Every demo pay day from 2024 to 2035 is on a working day of the federal calendar, and a pay day on a weekend or holiday moves to the working day before
  19. BUILT 2026-09-30 by etyme-money: a worker’s hours this month are the days of the month, not the weeks that start in it (hoursInMonth in lib/periods), and a person paid through her own company is told her company bills and the buyer pays its invoice, never that wages are owed (workerPaidAs and ownCompanyBillsSays in lib/money/paid-through). OPEN: the worker’s page reads none of the three until etyme-supply wires them into /api/me/work and lib/consultant-portfolio — sent as exact changes
  20. FIXED 2026-10-06 by etyme-money: the first pay day on a line covers no more days than every later one does — the gap to the next pay day — even where the line started months before it. An award for work already under way writes no pay day already past, so its first pay day can sit long after the start; counted from the start it was given to an early period, and a run for the period it actually pays settled nothing

SUPERSEDED 2026-09-22 by the founder, after a second conversation with the CTO of the two-billion-dollar company: without SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 there is almost no chance of an enterprise contract. The line below said this starts after the first contract that requires it. That was right about not buying an attestation ahead of a buyer and wrong about the order, because the buyer is asking for it before he will sign anything at all — for this buyer the attestation is Phase 1, not Phase 3.
  19. What that changes, and it is one thing: Type II attests that controls OPERATED over a window, commonly six months, so the window is the long pole and it is the only part that cannot be compressed later. Starting the observation clock costs little and shortens nothing if it is deferred. Type I is a point-in-time assessment of design, takes weeks, and is the bridge a buyer accepts meanwhile. The penetration test still runs first, because a report written over controls nobody has attacked is the wrong order.
  20. Worth one check before the money: this is one buyer describing his own procurement, and he is very likely right about it. Two or three of the hundred leads asked the same question would say whether it is the market or the man.
  21. What is already evidence, and it is unusual: the access log with refusals, the automation ladder, retention as code with the legal basis cited, erasure, the breach clock and the two deploy gates were all built for their own reasons and are most of what an auditor asks to see operating. Most firms start this with nothing and collect for six months. That is the one place this row is ahead rather than behind.
  22. The old sequencing line, kept because it was written down confidently and is half wrong: “this starts after the first contract that requires it, and never before the pen test. An attestation bought ahead of a buyer is a year of cost with nobody on the other side of it, and a report written over controls a pen test has not been run against is the wrong order.”

That was replaced in the morning by its opposite — the incumbents’ program offices are who Etyme is measured against — and the founder replaced THAT the same day, in these words: “MSP selling should be undercover selling and more as value addition rather than fully pitching for the market. Remove the threat if any to supply chain.” So the rivalry framing is gone and nothing replaces it: the record is what the page sells, the program office appears once as a quiet second way to use it, never as a headline, never sized against anybody, never as a new category. Nothing on any page, letter or screen reads as a threat to a supplier — its rates and its sub-vendors’ names stay private, its client stays its client, Etyme never supplies a person, and a program Etyme runs is said to make a supplier’s life easier rather than to watch it. A sentence a supplier would read as aimed at them is removed, and lib/positioning holds a guard for it. Both earlier versions are kept here because each was written down confidently and each was wrong within hours; a row that shows only the latest teaches nobody that.
  23. The sequencing, decided 2026-09-20 and reversed the same day by the founder, whose call it is: Etyme is a program office provider, and this row is the offer rather than a note about one. CLAUDE.md carries the decision — “The client chooses one of two, in the founder’s words (2026-09-20): Etyme as VMS software, where the client’s own program office runs the program on Etyme; or Etyme as MSP provider, where Etyme’s program office runs it for them on the same software.” Both stand on the same record, a screen offering the choice uses those two labels because a buyer knows them, and the category sentence still comes first. The earlier note on this row said “not now; after the first paying client” and it is superseded, not softened — kept here only so nobody re-derives it from a chat log.
